---
title: "Grants as code: compiled budgets, funder views, and machine-checkable applications"
author:
  - name: Max Ghenis
    affiliations: [PolicyEngine, The Axiom Foundation]
date: 2026-08-14
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
abstract: >
  Grant applications are assembled by hand from three kinds of material that
  organizations already hold in structured form: the work they intend to do,
  the cost of the people and systems that do it, and the rules of the funder's
  form. We describe a pipeline that treats each as data — a priced menu of
  work items with machine-checkable completion evidence; personnel rates
  derived from encoded tax and retirement law with benchmark provenance;
  funder proposals as selections over the shared menu, with co-funding
  fractions that make cross-application double-billing a pre-award,
  machine-checked invariant; and versioned funder packs that validate and
  assemble the application in continuous integration. We situate the pipeline
  against six adjacent tool landscapes and identify which components are new.
  All components are open source. [DRAFT — abstract rewrites after the
  landscape section lands.]
---

# The claims {#sec-claims}

The paper stands or falls on six claims. Each is falsifiable against the
landscape; the research pass is instructed to kill any with prior art, and
verdicts (NOVEL / PARTIAL / EXISTS) flow into @sec-landscape.

**C1 — Budgets as compiled artifacts.** A grant budget should be the output
of a pure function over (menu items, rates, selection), reproducible in CI,
not a spreadsheet edited toward a total. Changing a rate or a selection
regenerates every downstream table identically — in the proposal document,
the funder deck, and the org's public planning pages.

**C2 — The pre-award double-billing gate.** When proposals are selections
with per-item co-funding fractions, "no item is more than 100% funded across
simultaneous applications" becomes a machine-checked invariant at draft time.
Federal post-award machinery (2 CFR 200 effort certification) attests this
retrospectively and manually; we know of no pre-award, automatic equivalent.
[Verify against landscape lane 4.]

**C3 — Rule-derived personnel rates.** Loaded personnel costs computed from
encoded law — employer payroll taxes by jurisdiction, retirement contribution
caps (IRS §415(c)/§402(g)), benefit schedules — rather than flat multipliers,
with market benchmarks (BLS OES, sourced percentiles) attached per role. The
budget's comp-justification appendix becomes a generated artifact.

**C4 — Funder-as-view.** One organizational substrate (the menu), many
proposals as selections over it. The org maintains its work-item database
once; each funder sees a view: selected items, fractions, an org-base
allocation, a window. Views make co-funding legible instead of narrative.

**C5 — Funder packs: the application as a checked build.** Funder form rules
— section structure, word/character/page limits, budget caps, required
attachments, placeholder gates — as versioned code; the application repo
builds in CI to a status artifact and an assembled document. (Shipped today
in grantkit 0.2.x; the claim to test is whether anyone else does this.)

**C6 — The configurator.** Because budgets compile (C1), a funder can be
handed the model itself: presets and toggles over the same menu and rates the
organization runs on, every configuration inside adjudicated bounds. Scenario
pressure-testing becomes something the funder does live, not a static
appendix.

The through-line — and the paper's one-sentence thesis: **the grant pipeline
inherits the properties of the software pipeline the moment its inputs become
data: reproducibility, diffability, invariants checked before submission
instead of audited after award.**

# The pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

[Architecture section. Layers, each stateless, org data in org repos:

1. **Rates** — eggnest-employer: scenario.yaml (org defaults: retirement
   rate and caps, employer tax state, benefit schedules; roles with SOC
   codes and salaries; benchmark CSV with sourced percentiles) → rates
   export. The Axiom Foundation 2026 scenario is the running example.
2. **Menu** — priced work items: type, one-sentence what, machine-checkable
   done-evidence, resourcing (FTE-months by role, encoding modules, contract
   dollars), dependencies, revenue linkage, provenance. Seeded 24 items from
   the Axiom diligence corpus; schema in axiom-roadmap-dashboard PR #2,
   migrating to grantkit-canonical YAML.
3. **Views** — selections with fractions + org-base allocation. Worked
   examples: a $2M concept note priced at 134% of target on first selection
   (the trim made visible pre-submission); a three-level funder structure as
   three nested views.
4. **grantkit budget** — tables, caps, the C2 gate. **grantkit check/build**
   — packs, placeholders, assembly, status.json. CI runs both; the funder
   sees the same numbers the org plans by.
5. **Configurator** — interactive surface over 1–4.

Include the reproduction block: every table in this paper regenerates from
the fixture scenario + menu via `grantkit budget`; the paper is its own CI
check (C1 demonstrated by construction).]

# Case study {#sec-case}

[The August 2026 diligence sprint, anonymized where required: a bottoms-up
org model derived four coherent org shapes ($21.2M–$37.8M five-year) from one
rates+items substrate in an evening; the same substrate priced a $2M concept
note, exposed a 34% overshoot before submission, produced funder-level
presets, and surfaced one leadership pricing decision (levy vs full-price
attestation posture) that a spreadsheet workflow had left implicit for weeks.
Numbers policy applies; co-funder names only where already public.]

# What this does not solve {#sec-limits}

[Honest boundary section, in the house style of volunteered scope carve-outs:
narrative quality is untouched (the prose is still written, by people or
models — the pipeline only guarantees the prose sits on true numbers);
relationship work is untouched; menus can be gamed by the org itself (garbage
items in, plausible budget out) — the gates check consistency, not wisdom;
funder adoption of configurators is untested beyond one live diligence;
rule-derived rates currently cover US federal + state payroll/retirement law
only.]
